CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Proceed with announced retaliatory tariffs on $50B of US goods as the first tranche takes effect July 6. Simultaneously open back-channel diplomatic communication and file WTO complaints to signal willingness to de-escalate within a rules-based framework. Do not voluntarily escalate beyond the already-announced retaliation, but do not concede before talks have begun.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading of +0.6 reflects multiple converging pressures on China's position. First, the ZTE denial order (April 16) exposed a critical structural vulnerability: fewer than 8% of chips used in China are domestically manufactured, and China imported $260B in ICs in 2017 (web_search: CSIA data). This means the US can weaponize supply chains against China's tech sector in ways China cannot symmetrically counter. Second, the escalation asymmetry is severe: Trump directed USTR on June 18 to identify an additional ~$200B of Chinese imports for tariffs if China retaliates, while China imports only ~$130B from the US total, meaning China cannot match further US escalation (event_timeline: 2018-06-18). Third, the yuan fell 3.25% in June — its worst monthly depreciation in 25 years — raising the specter of capital outflows and financial instability reminiscent of August 2015 (web_search: CNBC, WSJ reports). Chinese equities entered bear territory with a 7.5% decline. Fourth, the $50B tariff lists specifically target Made in China 2025 sectors (aerospace, ICT, robotics, machinery), directly threatening China's industrial upgrading strategy (event_timeline: 2018-04-03, 2018-06-15).

However, the situation is not yet existential (+1.0). China's macro indicators remain functional: industrial production growth is stable around 6.7-6.8%, CPI is moderate at ~1.8%, and PBOC has room to ease via reserve requirement cuts (country_health: CHN indicators). China can redirect soybean purchases to Brazil and Argentina, mitigating agricultural retaliation leverage. The May 19 joint statement showed diplomacy can work, even though the truce collapsed on May 29. China can also rally domestic nationalism around tech self-sufficiency — the ZTE ban has already accelerated semiconductor investment plans with a ~$24B second fund (web_search: ChinaMoneyNetwork).

The action score of -0.3 reflects a retaliatory stance that is necessary but calibrated. Retaliation is essential: China must demonstrate it will not absorb tariffs passively, both for domestic political legitimacy and to establish deterrence. The matching $50B response (announced June 15) is proportionate and already committed. However, pursuing further escalation beyond matching retaliation would be unwise given the asymmetry — the US can escalate to $250B+ while China's total US imports are ~$130B. Retaliation paired with WTO filings and diplomatic signaling preserves China's position as defender of the multilateral trade order (a useful narrative with EU and other allies also facing US tariffs on steel/aluminum) while leaving a path to negotiation open. The key second-order risk is that retaliation triggers the $200B escalation, but conceding without a fight would be worse — it would signal weakness and invite further demands on Made in China 2025 and state subsidies.
key_factors: ZTE denial order exposed critical semiconductor dependency (8% domestic, $260B IC imports)
Escalation asymmetry: US threatens $200B+ more; China imports only ~$130B total from US
Yuan depreciated 3.25% in June (worst month in 25 years), capital outflow risk rising
$50B tariffs target Made in China 2025 sectors directly
Chinese equities in bear territory (-7.5%), financial stability concerns
China macro still functional: IP stable, CPI moderate, PBOC has easing room
Soybean retaliation leverage limited by Brazil/Argentina substitution
EU aligning with China against US protectionism — alliance opportunity

sources_cited.excerpt: US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
Trump directs USTR to identify an additional ~$200B of Chinese imports for 10% tariffs if China retaliates against the $50B action.
USTR announces final two-stage $50B tariff plan: 25% on List 1 (~$34B, 818 lines, effective July 6) and List 2 (~$16B, later). China announces matching retaliation the same day.
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
Fewer than 8 percent of the chips used in China are manufactured by domestic Chinese companies. China imported ICs to the value of $260.14 billion in 2017.
The yuan's 3.25 percent fall in June has drawn comparisons to August 2015 when the central bank unexpectedly allowed the currency to weaken nearly 3 percent against the U.S. dollar.
China industrial production stable, CPI moderate ~1.8%, PBOC has room to adjust reserve requirements.
